ratings.text:
Lead upright,
the ranks fall in.
ratings.reasons: 13 and 18 characters, 6 words. With the verb first the instruction is clear, and line 2 names what the viewer sees: the ragged ranks fall in one at a time, nearest the general first, after he brightens. Leader and result read as cause and effect. Faithful to the Tuan (能以眾正, able to make the many upright). It leaves out the Image's care for the people, which is acceptable in one sentence.

ratings.text:
High and low talk:
that is peace.
ratings.reasons: Unchanged from round 1 (8). Line 1 is 18 characters, the limit. Faithful to the Image, and it fits the picture: the two trigrams meet and the seam flashes. It still defines peace rather than asking something of the viewer, and now 12, its pair, asks for something while 11 does not. This is the only difference in the pair. One of three colon lines in the set (11, 12, 27); three is the most the set should carry.

ratings.text:
High and low part:
turn down rewards.
ratings.reasons: 18 and 18 characters, 7 words, both at the limit. It keeps the 11 parallel and now carries the Image's ask (不可榮以祿, take no honours or pay). The link between the two halves is left for the viewer to make: when high and low have stopped talking, taking the system's pay endorses it. A newcomer may pause on whose rewards, but the dimming, parting picture says pull inward, which supports it. Passes.

16 and 10 characters, 5 words. Line 2 is now the picture's own move: the one yang line, third place, steps back and dims. 'The most' is still unspecified (money? merit?), but with the one bright line standing out among the yin it reads as the one with the most to show, which is Wang Bi's reading of line 3 (勞謙君子). Plain, and a newcomer gets the ask.

ratings.text:
Once you stray,
come back soon.
ratings.reasons: 15 and 15 characters, 6 words; faithful to line 1 (不遠復) and it fits the line that splits, dims and rejoins with a flash. But 'come back soon' is a stock farewell (shop signs, goodbyes), and many viewers will hear it that way, as an invitation rather than a correction. 'Soon' also loses the source's point, which is returning before you have gone far. 'Turn back' names the hexagram's move, and 'at once' carries 'not far'.
ratings.rewrite:
Once you stray,
turn back at once.

ratings.text:
Guard your mouth:
food and words.
ratings.reasons: Unchanged from round 1 (8). 17 and 15 characters, 6 words. Faithful to the Image (careful with speech, moderate in eating and drinking), and the lower jaw rising twice under the still upper jaw now reads as chewing, so text and picture hold each other. Colon form shared with 11 and 12.

ratings.text:
The beam sags.
Shore it up now.
ratings.reasons: 14 and 16 characters, 7 words, and 'shore it up' is better than round 1's 'act now'. But the picture does not show a sag: the four middle lines brighten and spread, and the weak end lines bend away from them, like ties on a bundle too thick for them. The viewer is told 'sags' and sees ends splaying. The Tuan explains the sag as exactly that (棟橈，本末弱也, the ridgepole sags: root and tip are weak), and Wang Bi's lines 2 to 4 praise the one who rescues the weak (拯弱興衰; 能拯其弱…棟隆吉). Name the weak ends the viewer watches give way and ask them to brace them. That is still the Judgment's 'going forward is supported', as a concrete act. Source becomes the Tuan on 28 with Wang Bi on lines 2 to 4.
ratings.rewrite:
The ends give way.
Brace them now.

ratings.text:
Like fire, cling
to what is right.
ratings.reasons: 16 and 17 characters, 7 words. 'Cling' is the hexagram's name and the Tuan's verb (柔麗乎中正), and 'what is right' is plain for 中正. The picture carries it well: each centre warms to amber and the amber takes the lines it clings to, and the two centres stay lit. The break splits 'cling / to', which round 1 marked down in 24 and 51. Here 'Like fire, cling' reads as a complete imperative and line 2 completes it without changing its sense, unlike 'Look / at'. Acceptable.

16 and 16 characters, 5 words. It now covers both halves of the Judgment: proclaimed at court (openly) and resorting to arms not supported (unarmed). It fits the picture: the glow climbs the five yang and the one yin at the top parts and fades. Two stacked adverbs make line 2 terse, and 'unarmed' is a little stiff, but it is literal to 不利即戎, and no rewrite within 18 characters says both halves more plainly.

ratings.text:
Check a bad start
while it's small.
ratings.reasons: Unchanged from round 1 (9). Both lines 17 characters, 7 words. 'Check' is the metal brake of line 1, and Wang Bi's stop it at its start. The picture shows it: the yin rises, the line above flashes and holds it, and it settles back and dims. It is the clearest ask in the set.

12 and 17 characters, 5 words, and the 'X? Y.' form is gone. But 'look at yourself' is a common rebuke in English ('look at yourself!'), and it can read as scolding rather than the Image's calm self-examination (恐懼修省, use fear and trembling to examine yourself). The source's own verb is plain, fits in 16 characters, and matches the picture, where the shock runs up both trigrams and nothing moves.

ratings.text:
No hidden aim,
firm at the core.
ratings.reasons: 14 and 17 characters, 7 words. 'No hidden aim' is plain and from line 1 (having something else brings no peace), and the picture's open centre, where the two yin lines part, now reads as nothing hidden. Line 2 matches the second and fifth lines brightening (剛得中). Two verbless phrases describe a person rather than tell the viewer to do something, but a newcomer gets the intent: sincerity, with nothing held back.
